---
title: "Sample spaces"
---

Suppose that we want to describe the form of one English personal pronoun token. We may eventually want to ask whether the form is nominative, accusative, singular, or plural. Before we can ask any of those questions, however, we need to decide what one possible result of the observation looks like.

This is a representation problem. A recording may contain *them*, a transcript may contain the spelling `them`, and an annotation may contain the label `third person plural accusative`. Each record describes the same token at a different level. A probability model must commit to one of those levels.

::: {.callout-note title="Assumed background"}
This module assumes the basic set theory reviewed in [*Languages as formal objects*](https://aaronstevenwhite.io/intro-to-cl/languages-as-formal-objects/). In particular, you should already be comfortable with sets, membership, subsets, power sets, union, intersection, difference, and complement. We will use these ideas to define probability spaces rather than reintroducing them here.
:::

We will begin with the surface form. One possible list is

$$
\Omega
=\{\textit{I},\textit{me},\textit{you},\textit{he},\textit{him},
\textit{she},\textit{her},\textit{we},\textit{us},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.
$$

The symbol $\Omega$ denotes the [**sample space**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html). Each member of $\Omega$ is an [**outcome**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html). If the recorded form is *her*, the realized outcome is one member of the sample space.

We can now state the definition.

> A sample space $\Omega$ is the set of outcomes represented by a probability model.

The word *represented* matters. This sample space does not claim that English has exactly eleven pronouns. It omits reflexive forms, possessive forms, and dialectal variants. Those omissions might be harmless for a study of nominative and accusative personal pronouns. They would make the space unusable for a study of reflexive choice.

## Check the representation by hand

At this stage, we have not assigned probabilities. We can only ask whether a proposed outcome belongs to the sample space. The notation $x\in\Omega$ says that $x$ is a member of $\Omega$, while $x\notin\Omega$ says that it is not.

For the space above,

$$
\textit{him}\in\Omega
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\textit{herself}\notin\Omega.
$$

Work through what these statements mean. The first says that the model has a possible result corresponding to *him*. The second says that the model has no possible result corresponding to *herself*. It does not say that speakers cannot produce *herself*.

A minimal base R representation makes the same membership check.

```{r}
#| eval: false
omega <- c("I", "me", "you", "he", "him", "she", "her",
           "we", "us", "they", "them")

"him" %in% omega
"herself" %in% omega
```

The first expression returns `TRUE`; the second returns `FALSE`. The code is only a finite encoding of the set written above. It does not yet define which outcomes are common.

## Granularity changes the outcome

Now consider a vowel production study. At least three sample spaces are possible.

1. One outcome is an entire recording.
2. One outcome is a segmented vowel token.
3. One outcome is an acoustic measurement taken at a specified point in a vowel.

These spaces do not give three interchangeable descriptions of one observation. They answer the question “what could happen once?” differently.

Suppose a speaker produces *heed* twice and we measure F1 at the vowel midpoint. Under the second representation, the two vowel tokens are two possible observed units. Under the third representation, values such as 285 Hz and 301 Hz are possible observed results. A question about whether the vowel was /i/ belongs naturally to the token representation. A question about whether F1 was below 300 Hz belongs naturally to the measurement representation.

This choice also determines what must accompany the observed value. In a judgment experiment, the response value `6` alone may not identify the outcome that matters for analysis. We may instead represent an outcome as the pair

$$
\langle\text{participant and sentence trial},\ 6\rangle.
$$

The sample space should contain the distinctions needed by the linguistic question.

## A common failure: treating omission as impossibility

An omitted outcome is not an impossible result. A space may appear complete because every listed outcome is assigned a place, even though the list omits results that the observation process can produce.

For instance, a forced choice experiment may offer the responses *agent* and *patient*. If participants can also skip the trial, then

$$
\Omega=\{\text{agent},\text{patient}\}
$$

does not represent the recorded process unless skipped trials are removed by an explicit rule. A model using this space cannot distinguish a skipped response from missing data created later in processing.

The repair is not to add every conceivable linguistic object. It is to state the observation process and include every result that process can deliver for the question at hand.

## Check your understanding

1. A study records a seven point judgment for each participant and sentence. Give one sample space whose outcomes are response values. Then give a different sample space whose outcomes retain trial identity.
2. In the pronoun space above, what does $\textit{herself}\notin\Omega$ claim about the model? What does it not claim about English?
3. A corpus annotation distinguishes nouns, verbs, and adjectives but labels every other token `OTHER`. Is `OTHER` an outcome? Explain your answer from the stored annotation process.
4. A vowel study stores one F1 trajectory with eleven time points for each token. What question would make one trajectory a suitable outcome? What different question would make one time point a suitable outcome?

Once we know what can happen once, we can group outcomes that give the same answer to a linguistic question. The [next page](events.qmd) introduces those groups as events.
